title: Chapter XXII
focus: a letter, a secret and the wedding

teacherSummary.text: Victor recovers in Paris with his father, who takes his claim that he murdered William, Justine and Clerval as delirium. Elizabeth writes asking whether he loves someone else; Victor answers that he has one dreadful secret, which he will confide to her the day after their marriage. Remembering the creature's threat (“I will be with you on your wedding night”), he assumes he himself is the target and carries pistols and a dagger. Back in Geneva the wedding is fixed; after the ceremony the couple sail across the lake to spend the night at Evian, and the chapter ends as they near the shore at sunset.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XXII,” how does Shelley show a letter, a secret and the wedding? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXII, how does Shelley develop the idea of a letter, a secret and the wedding? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXII develops the idea of a letter, a secret and the wedding. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of a letter, a secret and the wedding. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXII suggests about a letter, a secret and the wedding. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's foreshadowing and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter XXII to complicate the reader's understanding of a letter, a secret and the wedding. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a letter, a secret and the wedding responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of a letter, a secret and the wedding follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXII and its treatment of a letter, a secret and the wedding. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's foreshadowing and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXII as evidence for a larger claim about a letter, a secret and the wedding in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a letter, a secret and the wedding. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Victor misread the creature's threat, and what does that reveal about him? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are overtaxed, unchained, obliterate, amphitheatre, playmate. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “I soon found that I had overtaxed my strength, and that I must repose before I could continue my journey.” In this sentence it means: strained by asking too much of. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Weddings in this social class involved property arrangements; the Frankensteins regain some of Elizabeth's inheritance. Why does this chapter matter? Dramatic irony: readers can see that the threat may be aimed at Elizabeth, while Victor thinks only of his own danger. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “My father yielded at length to my desire to avoid society, and strove by various arguments to banish my despair.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to a letter, a secret and the wedding? I circle “futility”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find foreshadowing, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: My father yielded at length to my desire to avoid society, and strove by various arguments to banish my despair. Sometimes he thought that I felt deeply the degradation of being obliged to answer a charge of murder, and he endeavoured to prove to me the futility of pride.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Foreshadowing, Irony, Characterization: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Chapter XXII develops the idea of a letter, a secret and the wedding. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about a letter, a secret and the wedding, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes a letter, a secret and the wedding. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
